title: vi, vim and neovim
summary: Which one you are actually running, what differs, and the few commands that work in all of them.

steps.title: A family of editors
body: - **vi** (1976) is the original, part of the POSIX standard. Every Unix-like system ships *a* `vi`.

- **vim** ("Vi IMproved", 1991) adds undo history, visual mode, syntax colouring, splits, plugins. On most distros `vi` is actually vim, sometimes a minimal build (`vim-tiny` on Debian/Ubuntu) that behaves more like classic vi.
- **neovim** (`nvim`, 2015) is a fork of vim with Lua configuration, a built-in LSP client and better defaults. Its config lives in `~/.config/nvim/init.lua` (or `init.vim`).
- **BusyBox vi** is a tiny vi in Alpine and other minimal images: modes, `hjkl`, `dd`, `:wq` work, but no visual mode or multi-level undo.
Everything in this track's survival and motions lessons works in all of them.
> **Practise:** open **Labs → Vim & nano trainer** and run this lesson's challenges until the keys come without thinking.

steps.prompt: You are in a minimal Alpine container and `vim` is not found, but `vi` is. What are you running, and will `dd`, `i`, `:wq` work?
options: BusyBox vi; yes, the core keys all work
steps.explain: Alpine's `vi` is from BusyBox. It is small but supports the core commands, which is exactly why the core is worth knowing by heart.

steps.prompt: Match the editor to a fact about it.
pairs: in the POSIX standard, present on every Unix-like system
Vi IMproved: visual mode, undo tree, syntax, plugins
fork with Lua config and a built-in LSP client
tiny vi in Alpine and embedded systems
Debian/Ubuntu's minimal default build of vim

steps.title: Which one is it?
body: Inside vim, `:version` shows the build and the features compiled in (`+clipboard`, `-python3`, ...). `:help` is excellent: `:help dd`, `:help :wq`, `:help vimtutor`. And run `vimtutor` in a shell for a 30-minute built-in course.

steps.prompt: Works in BusyBox vi too, or needs vim/neovim?
Find out what `vi` really is on this box.
steps.explain: `command -v` prints the path a name resolves to; `readlink -f` follows every symlink to the real file.

steps.prompt: Where does neovim read its configuration from by default?
steps.explain: neovim follows the XDG base directory spec. It does not read `~/.vimrc` unless you source it.

steps.title: What is vi on this machine?
prompt: Before you write instructions for a box, find out what `vi` really is there. On Debian, `vi` is a symlink to `/etc/alternatives/vi`, which points at the real program.
1. Write the real file `vi` runs, after following **every** symlink, to `~/answers/vi-path.txt` (one line, the absolute path).

Useful: `type -a vi` (in this shell, `vi` is also a small function that explains why the full screen does not work here; the real program is the file), `ls -l`, `readlink -f`, `update-alternatives --display vi`.

checks.name: vi-path.txt names the real program
checks.fail: `~/answers/vi-path.txt` should hold the final target of the symlinks, the way `readlink -f /usr/bin/vi` prints it.

checks.name: vi-version.txt holds the version line
checks.fail: `~/answers/vi-version.txt` should be the first line of `vi --version` (`vi --version | head -n 1`).

hints: `type -a vi` lists the function and then `/usr/bin/vi`. `ls -l /usr/bin/vi` shows the first link.
`readlink -f /usr/bin/vi` follows every link to the end. `update-alternatives --display vi` shows the choices Debian knows about.
steps.explain: Here `vi` is full Vim (`vim.basic`, version 9.1), so text objects, `:s` with `\v` and macros all work. On Alpine the same command would show BusyBox, and in a minimal image `vim.tiny`: always check before you rely on a feature. `update-alternatives` is how Debian and Ubuntu choose which program answers to `vi` and `editor`.
